points: Galaxies gradually exhaust the gas available for making new stars.
The longest-lived small red dwarfs burn for trillions of years.
Eventually the last one fades and no new stars are possible.

beats.heading: The era of remnants
points: What remains are white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes.
They slowly cool and radiate away their heat.
Rare collisions produce brief flashes in an otherwise dark universe.

beats.heading: Black holes evaporate
points: Hawking radiation causes black holes to lose mass extraordinarily slowly.
The largest take unimaginable spans of time to disappear.
One by one, the last structures evaporate.

beats.heading: What is left
points: A thin, cold, expanding fog of particles and radiation.
No structure, no gradients, nothing capable of storing or using energy.
Every event that will ever happen has already happened.

beats.heading: Why this is not depressing
points: The interesting era is measured in tens of billions of years, and we are inside it.
Stars, planets and observers are only possible in this narrow window.
Being early is the good outcome.

topics.title: What Earth Actually Looks Like From the Space Station
topics.hook: There are people four hundred kilometres above you right now, watching the planet turn. They see a sunrise every forty-five minutes.
topics.promise: What the view is actually like, why it never gets old, and the one thing every astronaut says changes them.

beats.heading: Four hundred kilometres up
points: The International Space Station orbits roughly 400 kilometres above the surface.
That is close enough that Earth fills the window rather than looking like a globe.
You do not see the whole planet at once. You see coastlines, storms and mountain ranges sliding past.

beats.heading: Sixteen sunrises a day
points: The station circles the planet in about ninety minutes, travelling near 7.7 kilometres per second.
That means a sunrise and a sunset roughly every forty-five minutes.
Crews see about sixteen of each in every twenty-four hours.

beats.heading: The thin blue line
points: At the horizon the atmosphere shows up as a startlingly thin band of blue.
Almost all of the air that keeps us alive sits within the first few kilometres.
From orbit it looks less like a sky and more like a coat of paint.

beats.heading: The night side
points: On the dark half of each orbit the continents light up as networks of cities.
Coastlines and river valleys trace themselves in orange and white.
Lightning storms flicker under the clouds, sometimes hundreds at a time.

beats.heading: Aurora from above
points: Auroras are not overhead from the station. They are often below and alongside it.
Charged particles from the Sun spiral down the magnetic field and make the upper atmosphere glow.
Crews describe watching green curtains move beneath the spacecraft.

beats.heading: The effect it has
points: Astronauts repeatedly report a shift in perspective after seeing the planet whole and borderless.
It has a name in the literature: the orbital perspective, sometimes called the overview effect.
It is a consistent, documented reaction rather than a one-off poetic response.

topics.title: The Space Station Is Falling Right Now
topics.hook: The International Space Station is falling toward Earth continuously. It has been falling for over twenty-five years.
topics.promise: Why orbit is just falling that never lands, and what would happen if the station stopped being pushed.

beats.heading: Orbit is falling sideways
points: Gravity at the station's altitude is still about ninety percent of what you feel standing up.
The station is being pulled down constantly. It simply moves sideways fast enough that the surface curves away beneath it.
Weightlessness on board is not the absence of gravity. It is continuous free fall.

beats.heading: The air that should not be there
points: Even at 400 kilometres there are still traces of atmosphere.
That thin gas produces measurable drag, so the station loses altitude over time.
Left alone it would spiral down and re-enter.

beats.heading: It has to be pushed back up
points: Visiting spacecraft periodically boost the station to a higher orbit.
These reboosts are routine operations, not emergencies.
Without them the station's useful life would be measured in a few years, not decades.

beats.heading: Solar weather changes the schedule
points: When solar activity rises, the upper atmosphere heats and expands.
That increases drag at station altitude, so it descends faster.
Orbital maintenance is therefore tied to the Sun's eleven-year cycle.

beats.heading: How it will end
points: Agencies plan a controlled deorbit rather than letting it fall uncontrolled.
The station is far too large to burn up completely, so the debris path has to be aimed at open ocean.
It is the largest object humans have ever had to bring down deliberately.

topics.title: Every City on Earth, Seen From Orbit at Night
topics.hook: From orbit you can see where humanity lives. It is a surprisingly thin skin of light on a mostly dark planet.
topics.promise: What the night side of Earth reveals about us, and the patterns nobody expects to see.

beats.heading: The lit world is small
points: On the night side, populated regions appear as networks of orange and white light.
Enormous areas stay completely dark: oceans, deserts, forests, ice.
The lit fraction of the surface is far smaller than most people assume.

beats.heading: Coastlines draw themselves
points: Cities cluster along shorelines and rivers, so geography appears without any map.
The Nile shows up as a bright line through otherwise black desert.
Where people settled follows water almost everywhere.

beats.heading: Colour tells you the technology
points: Older sodium street lighting reads as orange, newer LED lighting as blue-white.
Satellite imagery over years shows cities shifting colour as lighting is replaced.
You can watch infrastructure change from orbit.

beats.heading: Lights with no city
points: Some bright spots sit far from any settlement: gas flares, fishing fleets, industrial sites.
Fleets using bright lamps to attract catch can appear as dense clusters at sea.
Not every light is a place where anyone lives.

beats.heading: Why it is measured
points: Night-light imagery is used to study urbanisation, energy use and disaster recovery.
A blackout after a storm is visible from orbit, and so is the recovery.
It is one of the few global datasets that updates nightly.

topics.title: What Happens to a Body After a Year in Orbit
topics.hook: Spend a year on the space station and you come back taller, with a weaker skeleton and eyes that have changed shape.
topics.promise: What a year of weightlessness measurably does to a person, and which changes do not fully reverse.

beats.heading: The spine unloads
points: Without gravity compressing them, spinal discs expand and astronauts measurably gain height.
The gain reverses after return, sometimes with back pain.
Post-flight injury risk stays elevated for a period.

beats.heading: Bone and muscle disappear
points: Weight-bearing bone can lose density at roughly one percent per month.
Muscle wastes fastest in the legs and lower back, which normally hold you upright.
Crews exercise around two hours a day purely to slow the loss.

beats.heading: Fluid moves to the head
points: Without gravity pulling blood downward, fluid shifts upward and faces look puffy.
Pressure changes appear to flatten the back of the eye, altering vision in many astronauts.
This is one of the better-documented and less-solved problems of long spaceflight.

beats.heading: Radiation adds up
points: Low Earth orbit still receives far more radiation than the ground.
The station is partly shielded by Earth's magnetic field; a Mars transit would not be.
Cumulative dose is a central limit on how long anyone can stay.

beats.heading: Down to gene expression
points: A twin study compared an astronaut in orbit with his identical twin on the ground.
Thousands of changes in gene expression were recorded, most reverting after return.
A minority took far longer to normalise, which is exactly why long-duration data matters.

topics.title: The Most Expensive Thing Ever Built Is Not On Earth
topics.hook: The most expensive single object humans have ever built is not a building or a ship. It is flying over your head at twenty-seven thousand kilometres an hour.
topics.promise: What it actually took to assemble a laboratory in orbit, piece by piece, without ever putting it together on the ground.

beats.heading: Built in pieces, in orbit
points: The station was launched as separate modules over more than a decade and assembled in space.
The complete structure was never assembled on the ground to check that it fit.
It spans roughly the area of a football field including its solar arrays.

beats.heading: The cost
points: Cost estimates across all partner agencies run to well over one hundred billion dollars.
That makes it the most expensive single object ever constructed.
The figure is spread across decades and many national budgets.

beats.heading: Continuously inhabited
points: People have lived aboard without a break since November 2000.
There has been no moment since then when all humans were on Earth.
Crews rotate, but the station is never left empty.

beats.heading: Everything has to be sent
points: Water is recycled aggressively, including from humidity and urine.
Air, food and spare parts arrive on scheduled cargo flights.
A supply failure is a genuine operational problem, not an inconvenience.

beats.heading: What it is actually for
points: It exists to run experiments that need sustained weightlessness — in biology, materials and fluid physics.
It is also the long-duration testbed for keeping people alive away from Earth.
Almost everything known about the human body in space over months came from here.
